summary: Point, command, watch, read: selection, the smart click, range and reachability, queueing, camera, and inspecting — the decisions every isometric, RTS, or ARPG control scheme has already made, written down once. Parts your game doesn't need switch off by answer.
mechanism: The mechanism is the loop from pointer input to world command to avatar action, together with the camera that frames it and the inspect channel that reads it. It owns which button carries which verb, what a command means on ground versus on an interactable, what happens when a command cannot be satisfied, whether commands queue, how the camera behaves, and how the player reads objects without acting on them.

It deliberately does NOT own feel: camera stiffness, easing, pathfinding algorithm, cursor art, and animation are the builder's craft. The boundary runs through the middle of the camera: which mode exists and which manual controls exist is convention and lives here; how the follow feels does not.

An interactable is a world object the game declares commandable; the interactables collection carries the classes. A command on an interactable is a request to perform that class's interaction; a command on ground is a request to move. Under a smart mapping one button carries both meanings, resolved by what is under the cursor.

Button roles decide which commands pointer presses request. Acceptance tests that begin with a move or interaction command enter at that command boundary; they do not imply that either pointer button produces the command. This keeps the other command rules explicit even when both pointer buttons carry none.
A rejected command changes no state: no avatar motion, no camera motion, no partial effect. Rejection must be observable to the player; its presentation is craft.
The inspect channel never changes world state. Reading is free, always.

decisions.question: What does the player select, and how does selection work?
decisions.rationale: A controller with no selection model has no one to command. One always-selected hero is the ARPG convention; groups are the classic RTS one.

options.meaning: One hero, always selected. There is no select action at all — every command goes to them. The ARPG way.
options.semantics: Exactly one avatar exists and is always selected. No selection action exists, no selection indicator is required, and no input can deselect. Every world command addresses the avatar.

options.meaning: Click a unit to select it; click empty ground to deselect. A command with nothing selected is refused.
options.semantics: One unit is selected at a time by a selection input on it; a selection input on empty ground deselects. Commands with nothing selected are rejected.

options.meaning: Drag a box, add to the selection, save numbered control groups. Commands go to the whole selection. The classic RTS way.
options.semantics: Multiple units select via drag-box and additive selection, with numbered control groups up to the group-count knob. Commands address the whole selection.

decisions.question: What does the primary pointer button do when pressed over the world?
decisions.rationale: This answer owns the primary button's world role. It does not judge whether the two buttons together make the game playable, and it does not constrain the button inside UI surfaces.

options.meaning: On ground it asks the avatar to move; on an interactable it requests that interaction. The thing under the pointer decides which command is issued.
options.semantics: Over ground, the primary button issues a move command toward the pointer position. Over an interactable, it requests that interaction and issues no move-only command.

options.meaning: It always issues a move command. Pressing it on an interactable requests movement there without requesting interaction.
options.semantics: The primary button always issues a move command toward the pointer position. Over an interactable it still moves there and issues no interaction request.

options.meaning: It always requests interaction. On empty ground the request is refused and nothing moves.
options.semantics: Over an interactable, the primary button requests that interaction and issues no move command. Over ground, the press is rejected with observable feedback and changes no world state.

options.meaning: Over the world it does nothing at all. It may still work inside menus and UI.
options.semantics: Pressed over the world, the primary button changes no state, changes no selection, and issues no command. It may still act inside UI surfaces.

decisions.question: What does the secondary pointer button do when pressed over the world?
decisions.rationale: This answer owns the secondary button's world role. Any pairing with the primary answer is legal, including two identical roles or two none answers; the contract records the design rather than judging it.

options.meaning: On ground it asks the avatar to move; on an interactable it requests that interaction. The thing under the pointer decides which command is issued.
options.semantics: Over ground, the secondary button issues a move command toward the pointer position. Over an interactable, it requests that interaction and issues no move-only command.

options.meaning: It always issues a move command. Pressing it on an interactable requests movement there without requesting interaction.
options.semantics: The secondary button always issues a move command toward the pointer position. Over an interactable it still moves there and issues no interaction request.

options.meaning: It always requests interaction. On empty ground the request is refused and nothing moves.
options.semantics: Over an interactable, the secondary button requests that interaction and issues no move command. Over ground, the press is rejected with observable feedback and changes no world state.

options.meaning: Over the world it does nothing at all. It may still work inside menus and UI.
options.semantics: Pressed over the world, the secondary button changes no state, changes no selection, and issues no command. It may still act inside UI surfaces.

decisions.question: What happens when the player commands an interactable that is too far away?

options.meaning: Nothing has a range: anything can be commanded from anywhere, or interactions happen only through menus.
options.semantics: No interaction has a range: every interactable is commandable from anywhere or interactions happen only through UI. All range templates are pruned.

options.meaning: Click it from across the map: the avatar walks over and does it on arrival. Distance is never a refusal.
options.semantics: The command is accepted from any distance: the avatar paths toward the interactable and performs the interaction on arrival. Distance is never grounds for rejection.

options.meaning: Too far means no: the command is refused with visible feedback and the player must move closer first.
options.semantics: The command is rejected with observable feedback and no state change. The player must move first.

decisions.question: What happens when the player clicks somewhere no path can reach?
decisions.rationale: Every pathing game meets an unreachable click; without an answer, two faithful builds diverge on the first blocked dune.

options.meaning: Click across the river: the avatar walks to the closest spot a path reaches and stops there.
options.semantics: The command is accepted and the avatar travels to the reachable point nearest the target, then stops. Nearest is measured in path distance; ties resolve by the game's declared tie-break.

options.meaning: The click is refused with visible feedback; the avatar does not move.
options.semantics: The command is rejected with observable feedback and no motion.

decisions.question: Does a new command replace the current one, or queue behind it?
decisions.rationale: Every controller answers this the moment a second click lands mid-travel. The guidance leans on the single-avatar case; queueing is the RTS production convention.

options.meaning: A new click wins instantly: the old path is dropped. No queue exists, ever.
options.semantics: A new command replaces the current one immediately: the path is abandoned, no queue exists, and no queued command is ever observable.

options.meaning: Hold the declared modifier to line commands up, capped by the queue-max knob. A plain click clears the line and takes over. The player can see the queue.
options.semantics: A declared modifier input appends commands up to the queue-max knob; an unmodified command clears the queue and replaces. Queue contents are observable to the player.

options.meaning: Same, with no cap.
options.semantics: A declared modifier input appends commands with no maximum queue length; an unmodified command clears the queue and replaces it. Queue contents are observable to the player.

decisions.question: What does the camera do — follow the avatar, or move freely?
decisions.rationale: Something has to frame the world.

options.meaning: Glued dead-center on the avatar (or the middle of the selection), always.
options.semantics: The camera is rigidly centered on the avatar (or selection centroid) at all times.

options.meaning: The camera trails the avatar with some give — they never leave the screen, and nothing can detach it. How the trailing feels is the builder's craft.
options.semantics: The camera follows the avatar continuously with craft-defined slack; the avatar never leaves the view, and no input detaches the camera from it.

options.meaning: The player drives the camera; it follows no one.
options.semantics: The camera is player-driven and does not follow.
options.rationale: If you pick this, give manual-camera-pan a real answer — with not-applicable there, nothing can move the camera at all. The machine cannot enforce this; the reviewer does.

options.meaning: Player-driven, plus a declared input that snaps back to the avatar or selection.
options.semantics: The camera is player-driven and does not follow. A declared input recenters it on the avatar or selection.

decisions.question: How can the player move the camera by hand?

options.meaning: No manual camera at all — it is fully automatic. Only coherent with the follow modes.
options.semantics: No manual pan: the camera is fully automatic and no input moves it. Coherent only with the follow modes.

options.meaning: Push the pointer to the screen edge and the camera pans.
options.semantics: The pointer at the view edge pans the camera.

options.meaning: Hold a declared button and drag the world.
options.semantics: A declared button drags the camera.

options.meaning: Declared keys pan the camera — WASD, arrows, whatever the game names.
options.semantics: Declared keys pan the camera.

options.meaning: Two or more of the above, listed in your game's prose.
options.semantics: Two or more of the above, enumerated in game prose.

decisions.question: How does the player read a world object without acting on it?

options.meaning: No per-object readout exists in this game.
options.semantics: No inspect channel: the world offers no per-object readout. All inspect templates are pruned.

options.meaning: Rest the pointer on a thing and its readout appears right there — no click, and nothing in the world changes.
options.semantics: Resting the pointer on an object shows its readout in place, with no click and no world-state change. Staging per inspect-staging.

options.meaning: A declared input opens the object's readout in a declared panel. That input does nothing else.
options.semantics: A declared input on an object opens its readout in a declared surface. The input carries no other verb.

options.meaning: A toggle enters inspect mode: pointing reads instead of commanding.
options.semantics: A declared toggle enters an inspect mode in which pointing reads instead of commanding.

decisions.question: Does the hover readout arrive all at once, or in stages?
decisions.rationale: Staging is a property of hover, so this question is only asked when the inspect channel is hover — otherwise it is pruned, unasked.

options.meaning: Everything appears at once on hover.
options.semantics: The full readout appears on hover at once.

options.meaning: Name and the key live number appear instantly; stats and flavor arrive after the stage2-delay-ms dwell. Live values tick in both stages.
options.semantics: A compact stage (name and the key live value) appears immediately; the full stage (stats, flavor) appears after the stage2-delay-ms knob of continuous hover. Live values tick in both stages.

decisions.question: Does the cursor change to show what a click here would do?
decisions.rationale: Even a never-changing cursor is a decision.

options.meaning: One cursor everywhere; the game signals what things do some other way.
options.semantics: One cursor everywhere; affordances are communicated by other means.

options.meaning: The cursor changes over each interactable class — each row declares its form — and over plain ground shows the ground form your game's prose declares.
options.semantics: The cursor's form follows what is under it, per the cursor member of the interactables collection. Over plain ground it takes a ground form the game MUST declare in its own prose; an undeclared ground form is the scope-by-implication this option forbids.

decisions.question: Does a click just beside an interactable still count as hitting it?
decisions.rationale: Two builds that disagree here disagree on every near-miss click.

options.meaning: What you see is what you hit: a click beside a crate is a ground click.
options.semantics: Hitboxes match visual bounds; a click beside an interactable is a ground command.

options.meaning: A click within the magnetism-radius-px of something interactable snaps to it — nearest wins. Ground clicks need clear space.
options.semantics: A pointer within the magnetism-radius-px knob of an interactable's bounds resolves to that interactable, nearest-first; ties resolve by the game's declared tie-break. Ground commands require clearing the radius.

group-count.description: Number of numbered control groups. Identity-bearing: adding groups changes the control surface, not the balance.

queue-max.description: Maximum queued commands. Identity-bearing: queue depth shapes how the game is played, not how hard it is.

stage2-delay-ms.description: Continuous-hover dwell before the full readout stage appears. Rebalance-safe feel timing.

magnetism-radius-px.description: Pointer-to-bounds distance within which a click resolves to the interactable, in device-independent pixels at reference zoom. Rebalance-safe.

invariants.message: a declared snap radius must be positive
a bounded queue of fewer than two commands is none-replace misspelled

interactables.description: The classes of commandable world objects; the game declares the rows, and this core fixes only their shape. An empty collection is legal: the controller is then movement, camera, and inspect alone.

id.description: Stable class name; the id command and diagnostic events carry.

interaction.description: Citation to the package prose section that defines what interacting with this class does. The contract routes the command; the game owns the meaning.

cursor.description: The cursor form shown over this class, a kebab-case name the game owns — cursor art is craft, so the contract requires the declaration, never the vocabulary. MUST be present exactly when cursor-context is context-cursor and absent otherwise.

templates.title: the primary button carries its declared world role

map.smart: the ground press issues exactly one move command toward that position, and the interactable press issues exactly one interaction request with no move-only command
map.move: both presses issue exactly one move command toward the pointer position, and neither issues an interaction request
map.interact: the interactable press issues exactly one interaction request with no move command, and the ground press is rejected with observable feedback and no world-state change
map.none: neither press issues a command or changes any state; the button may retain a declared function inside UI surfaces

test.given: the avatar idle, open ground at one pointer position and a declared interactable at another
when: the primary button is pressed over the ground position
the primary button is pressed over the interactable

templates.text: The primary button's world role is fixed by its answer: {{bind:role-result}}.

templates.title: the secondary button carries its declared world role

map.smart: the ground press issues exactly one move command toward that position, and the interactable press issues exactly one interaction request with no move-only command
map.move: both presses issue exactly one move command toward the pointer position, and neither issues an interaction request
map.interact: the interactable press issues exactly one interaction request with no move command, and the ground press is rejected with observable feedback and no world-state change
map.none: neither press issues a command or changes any state; the button may retain a declared function inside UI surfaces

test.given: the avatar idle, open ground at one pointer position and a declared interactable at another
when: the secondary button is pressed over the ground position
the secondary button is pressed over the interactable

templates.text: The secondary button's world role is fixed by its answer: {{bind:role-result}}.

templates.title: distance never refuses a command

test.given: an interactable far beyond interaction range with a valid path to it
when: an interaction command is issued on it from that distance
then: the command is accepted with no range rejection
the avatar paths to the interactable and performs its row's interaction on arrival
issuing a new command mid-approach resolves per the command-queueing answer

templates.text: Distance never refuses a command: the avatar approaches and interacts on arrival, and a mid-approach command resolves per the queueing answer.

templates.title: an unreachable target resolves without partial motion

map.nearest-reachable-point: the avatar travels to the nearest reachable point by path distance and stops there
map.reject-command: the command is refused with observable feedback and the avatar does not move

test.given: a move command targeting a position no path reaches
then: no partial or oscillating motion toward the unreachable target is observable afterward

templates.title: a second command replaces the first

test.given: the avatar mid-travel on a first command
when: a second world command is issued
then: the first command is abandoned immediately and the second takes effect
no queued command is observable in any state before, during, or after

templates.text: A second command replaces the first immediately; no queue is ever observable.

templates.title: hover reads in two stages and changes nothing

test.given: the pointer brought to rest on an inspectable object
when: hover begins and continues past the dwell named by {{knob-cite:stage2-delay-ms}}
then: the compact stage appears immediately on hover
the full stage appears when continuous hover reaches the key's dwell, and not before
live values tick in both stages
no world state changes at any point in the hover

templates.text: Hover reads instantly; depth arrives at the dwell named by {{knob-cite:stage2-delay-ms}}; reading never changes the world.

templates.title: a near-miss inside the snap radius resolves to the interactable

test.given: a pointer position outside an interactable's visual bounds but within the distance named by {{knob-cite:magnetism-radius-px}}, and a second position just beyond that distance
when: command target resolution is evaluated at each pointer position
then: the within-radius position resolves to the interactable
the beyond-radius position resolves to ground
with two interactables in radius the nearer wins, ties per the game's declared tie-break

templates.text: A near-miss inside the radius named by {{knob-cite:magnetism-radius-px}} snaps to the interactable; beyond it, the ground receives the command; among candidates the nearest wins.

templates.title: the follow camera never loses the avatar

test.given: the avatar traveling continuously across the world for a fixture route
when: no manual camera input is given (and none exists when manual-camera-pan is not-applicable)
then: the avatar remains within the view at every frame of the route
no input event detaches the camera from the avatar

templates.text: Under a follow mode the avatar never leaves the view and nothing detaches the camera; how the follow feels is the builder's craft and is not tested here.
